title: Allied species in distant regions retain nearly the same instincts

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Allied species in distant regions retain nearly the same instincts

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Closely allied but distinct species living in distant parts of the world under different conditions often retain nearly the same instincts, which is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: This theory is, also, strengthened by some few other facts in regard to instincts; as by that common case of closely allied, but certainly distinct, species, when inhabiting distant parts of the world and living under considerably different conditions of life, yet often retaining nearly the same instincts.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VII, “Instinct”; section “Summary”. Scope: allied animal species in different geographical regions (e.g. thrushes, wrens)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch07-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Phylogenetic comparative analyses are straightforward for behaviours represented in movement datasets. Coverage is too narrow to resolve the generalization over allied animals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify behavioural similarity among close relatives occupying different environments and compare phylogenetic versus environmental effects. Strong behavioural phylogenetic signal after environmental control supports inherited instinct.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similar unmeasured ecological pressures can mimic inheritance.

Many instincts lack standardized cross-species measurements.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.82
data adequacy: 0.54
discriminating power: 0.58
data existence: 0.76
analysis feasibility: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Trees plus foraging and movement data can test a bird subset of retained habits under different geographies. That is narrower than instincts in general, and the datasets do not contain most of the behaviors Darwin had in mind. Similar habits also do not discriminate inheritance from parallel selection, so the explanatory half of the claim stays weakly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare behavioral similarity of sister species that live in distant regions with the ecological distance between those regions. High similarity of nest, migration, or foraging habits despite different conditions supports retention from a common ancestor; behavior tracking local conditions rather than relatedness would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similar behavior can be shared selection in unmeasured niches rather than inheritance.

Thrushes and wrens illustrate a claim stated for allied animals generally.

Foraging traits and tracks are proxies; nest, song, and display instincts are mostly uncoded.
